newsitem.title: USA: Human Genome to get $9 mln for license.
newsitem.headline: Human Genome to get $9 mln for license.

text.p: Human Genome Sciences, Inc said Wednesday Pharmacia & Upjohn Inc will make license and research payments totaling $9.0 million over three years for a non-exclusive license to use Human Genome Sciences technology.
The payments will be made under a collaborative agreement to develop antimicrobial therapeutic and diagnostic products for human and animal use, Human Genome said.
These products will be based upon gene sequences from Staphylococcus aureus and selected genes of a pathogenic strain of Escherichia coli -- more commonly known as E. coli.
It pointed out these organisms cause a wide range of community and hospital-acquired infections, as well as serious infections in livestock.

Under the agreement, Pharmacia & Upjohn has been granted a license to use the genome sequences from Staphylococcus aureus and E. coli, together with Human Genome Sciences' proprietary bioinformatics resources, to identify potential new targets for the development of novel anti-infective, antibiotic and antifungal products, the company said.

It said Pharmacia & Upjohn has the option to obtain non-exclusive licenses to use genome sequences of other medically significant bacteria that Human Genome Sciences may independently generate and determine to license.
In addition to the agreed payments, Human Genome Sciences said, it will receive milestone payments during product development and royalties on net sales of any products resulting from the agreement.
It said Pharmacia & Upjohn has an option to extend the agreement for up to two additional years at an undisclosed cost.

Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent cause of infections in hospitals and is the major cause of bacteremia, septic shock, wound infections and such serious metastatic infections as endocarditis and osteomyelitis.

Pathogenic E. coli is responsible for, or contributes to, a wide range of infectious diseases in humans, including urinary tract infections, intestinal infections, septic abscesses, intra-abdominal infections, endocarditis, pneumonia, sinusitis and food poisoning. The seriousness of these conditions makes the development of novel antibiotics medically imperative.

Because the symptoms of these diseases are often non-specific, accurate diagnosis usually requires culturing samples in order to identify the specific micro-organism involved and thereby determine which antibiotic is needed. This often takes days or even weeks.
Thus a diagnostic test that is both fast and highly specific for these pathogens would lead to more timely diagnosis and treatment, Human Genome Sciences said.
